extracted.intended_audience: PR professionals, corporate communicators, and press-release writers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for writing anecdotal (human-centered) leads in press releases: how to choose a person, structure the opening anecdote, and pivot to the news so reporters and editors will pick it up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find a "Poster Person"
rubrics_metrics.description: A single human being who can stand for your point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practice: Don't lead with numbers — lead with a person. Choose one person who embodies the story or issue so reporters can connect emotionally and narratively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interesting
rubrics_metrics.description: Must Be: Interesting
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lead should capture attention; select an anecdote that is inherently engaging or surprising so it draws readers in immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closely illustrative of broader point
rubrics_metrics.description: Must Be: Closely illustrative of broader point
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The anecdote must clearly exemplify the larger news or theme the release is advancing — it should feel representative, not tangential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific (not generic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Must Be: Specific (not generic)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vague, generic phrasing. Use a single concrete human moment or detail rather than abstract descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Must Be: Concrete detail
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include sensory and specific details (what was seen, heard, tasted, smelled, felt) to make the scene vivid and memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifiable (real person, real situation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Must Be: Verifiable (real person, real situation)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The anecdote should be fact-checkable — a real person and a real, confirmable situation — so reporters can trust and use the material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connect to broader significance/news within first few sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Followed By: Broader significance explained within first few sentences; connects to broader news within 3 sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the anecdote, quickly explain why the story matters and tie it explicitly to the news angle or announcement within the first 2–3 sentences so the narrative isn't left dangling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection to news angle
rubrics_metrics.description: Followed By: Connection to news angle
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the relationship between the anecdote and the release's news/announcement explicit — show how the person or moment illustrates the announcement's importance or impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pivot to data/announcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Followed By: Pivot to data/announcement; pivots smoothly to news
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After establishing the anecdote and broader significance, transition to the factual announcement or supporting data. The pivot should be smooth and logical, not abrupt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bigger picture
rubrics_metrics.description: Followed By: Bigger picture
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situate the news within a larger context — trends, implications, or why this matters beyond the single anecdote — to give editors story angles for coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern / Example Structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Pattern: 1. Specific human moment 2. Sensory/specific details 3. Pivot to news connection 4. Broader announcement
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this sequence as a practical template: open with a concrete moment, add sensory detail, connect that moment to the news, then state the announcement or larger significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hooks reader in first sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit Lead Quality Rubric: Hooks reader in first sentence
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opening sentence should immediately grab attention — the anecdote itself often serves this function for feature-style leads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoids lead-burying clichés
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit Lead Quality Rubric: Avoids lead-burying clichés (e.g., "In a move that...")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steer clear of overused, passive, or formulaic openings that bury the story or sound like corporate boilerplate; choose fresh, active phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uses active voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit Lead Quality Rubric: Uses active voice
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer active constructions to make the lead immediate and vivid; passive voice weakens the hook and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sets appropriate tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit Lead Quality Rubric: Sets appropriate tone
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lead should establish the tone (human-interest, celebratory, urgent, etc.) appropriate to the news and the target publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit Lead Quality Rubric: Audience-appropriate
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor the anecdote and language to the audience and outlet — what works for a magazine feature may not suit a trade outlet or local paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anecdotal (lead type)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anecdotal: Story-based opening; specific person/situation; sensory details
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best for feature-style stories, human interest, cause-related releases, long-form releases, and magazine-style outlets. Anecdotal leads are easier to believe, understand, and remember — they often outperform statistics for engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: News (Direct) (lead type)
rubrics_metrics.description: News (Direct): Straight news in first sentence; inverted pyramid
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use for breaking news, wire-style pickup, earnings/financial releases, crisis communications, and time-sensitive announcements where the most important facts must appear immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question (lead type)
rubrics_metrics.description: Question: Provocative question that hooks reader curiosity
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best for thought leadership pieces where inviting the reader to consider an issue is the primary objective; not ideal for hard-news announcements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quote (lead type)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quote: Compelling quote first that sets tone immediately
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works when a memorable, authoritative, or surprising quote encapsulates the story; best for major statements or personality-driven releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data/Stat (lead type)
rubrics_metrics.description: Data/Stat: Striking number in the lead (e.g., "1 in 4 Americans...")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective for survey or research releases; use when a striking statistic is the clearest hook and you have robust, credible data to back it up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene (lead type)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scene: Vivid scene-setting; cinematic opening
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best for feature-style coverage and outlets that favor narrative storytelling; a scene-setting lead works when describing place and atmosphere helps illustrate the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to Use anecdotal leads
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate contexts: Feature-style stories, human interest angles, cause-related releases, long-form releases, magazine-style outlets
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotal leads are most effective when the goal is engagement, empathy, or narrative storytelling rather than immediate fact dissemination.

rubrics_metrics.name: When NOT to Use anecdotal leads
rubrics_metrics.description: Not appropriate for: Breaking hard news, wire-style pickup, earnings/financial releases, crisis communications, time-sensitive announcements (use direct lead)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If speed, immediacy, or concise fact-first reporting is required, choose a direct/news lead instead of an anecdotal approach.
